blocks.label: How to use this paper
blocks.text: Open **Worked problems** and try each question on paper before revealing the steps. Where the official answer key has a mistake, the solution says so and shows the correct working.

worked.title: Q1 · Threshold choice and metrics (6 marks)

problem.text: Probabilities 0.90, 0.80, 0.70, 0.60, 0.55, 0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10, 0.05; true labels 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0. (a) Threshold 0.50, (b) threshold 0.30: confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1. (c) Which threshold for credit risk and for disease detection? Why may 0.50 be poor on imbalanced data?

steps.label: (a) 0.50
steps.text: Predicted 1 for the first five. TP = 3 (0.9, 0.8, 0.55), FP = 2 (0.7, 0.6), FN = 0, TN = 5.

steps.label: (b) 0.30
steps.text: Predicted 1 for the first seven: TP = 3, FP = 4, FN = 0, TN = 3.

steps.label: (c) Credit risk
steps.text: If "1" = risky borrower, missing a defaulter (FN) is costly, so lean to the **lower** threshold for high recall. If the cost is wrongly rejecting good customers (FP), keep 0.5 for precision. State your assumption.

steps.label: (c) Disease
steps.text: Missing a sick patient (FN) is the worst error, so use the **lower threshold (0.30)** to keep recall at 1, accepting more false alarms.

steps.label: (c) Imbalance
steps.text: Only 3 of 10 are positive. 0.5 assumes balanced classes and equal costs; a model on skewed data outputs lower probabilities for the rare class, so the best cut-off is usually below 0.5. Tune it on validation data (PR curve, F1 or cost).

worked.answer: 0.50: P 0.60, R 1.00, F1 0.75 · 0.30: P 0.43, R 1.00, F1 0.60. Here both thresholds catch all positives, so 0.50 is better on F1, but the decision depends on error costs.

worked.title: Q2 · Perceptron network for (x₁∧x₂)∨(x₃∧x₄) (5 marks)

problem.text: f(z) = 1 if z ≥ 0, else 0. (a) Decompose into hidden and output layers. (b) Derive AND and OR inequalities and weights. (c) Draw the network with final weights.

steps.label: (a) Decompose
steps.text: Hidden h₁ = x₁ AND x₂, h₂ = x₃ AND x₄; output F = h₁ OR h₂.

steps.label: (c) Network
steps.text: 4 inputs → 2 hidden units [h₁: weights (1, 1, 0, 0), b = −1.5; h₂: (0, 0, 1, 1), b = −1.5] → output [weights (1, 1), b = −0.5].

worked.answer: Hidden: two AND units (1, 1, −1.5); output: OR unit (1, 1, −0.5). Depth 2.

worked.title: Q3 · Forward and backward pass (8 marks)

steps.label: (d) Dead ReLU
steps.text: Neuron 2 has z⁽¹⁾ = −0.1 ≤ 0, so its derivative is 0: its error signal and all its incoming weight gradients are 0. It doesn't learn from this example; if that holds for all inputs it is a **dead ReLU** (fix: Leaky ReLU, better init, lower η).

worked.answer: Same network as the Chapter 5 numerical. The MLP lab reproduces every number.

steps.label: (c) Direction
steps.text: Distance to the optimum 4.47 → 3.20, so yes overall, though w₀ moved away (1 → 1.5 vs −1).

worked.title: Q5 · Overfitting and funnel architectures (5 marks)

problem.text: 500 samples, 20 features, regression. Model A: 6 hidden layers × 512 (train loss → 0, validation rises). Model B: 64 → 32 → 16 (moderate train, low validation).

steps.label: (a)
steps.text: Model A is **overfitting**: it memorises the training set (train ≈ 0, validation up). High variance.

steps.label: (b)
steps.text: Fewer/narrower layers (e.g. a funnel); dropout; L2 weight decay; batch norm; early stopping. (More data or augmentation helps too.)

steps.label: (e)
steps.text: Funnels compress progressively, forcing a compact representation that keeps only useful features. Far fewer parameters means less memorisation: 500/3,969 ≈ 0.13 samples per parameter for B vs 500/1.32M ≈ 0.0004 for A. (The Ch 5 sizing rule, parameters ≤ M/5 = 100, says even B is generous, so add regularisation.)
